newsitem.title: USA: UAW workers ratify pact to end 3-month GM strike.
newsitem.headline: UAW workers ratify pact to end 3-month GM strike.

text.p: Union workers from a General Motors Corp. full-size pickup truck plant overwhelmingly approved a tentative labour agreement Friday, ending one of the longest strikes in GM's history.

Production workers from United Auto Workers Local 594 voted by a 96.7 percent margin to return to work after nearly three months on the picket line. Skilled trade workers voted by an 86.7 percent margin to end the walkout, which began on April 22.
Local contract talks at GM's sprawling Pontiac complex broke down when the automaker refused union demands for more jobs and limits on shifting work to outside contractors.
The strike by about 4,100 hourly workers at the Pontiac East assembly plant had deprived GM of about 70,000 pickup trucks, most of which were profitable extended cab models.

Also on strike were 1,300 hourly employees who work at the nearby GM Truck Group product development and engineering facility, and about 400 workers from a Lear Corp. seating plant who are members of Local 594.
UAW leaders told members during a meeting at the Pontiac Silverdome Friday that GM agreed to add 557 new workers, including 275 skilled trade positions and 282 production jobs.
GM also agreed to pay out $4.5 million to settle grievances and other demands, as well as about $5 million to pay workers for the July 4 holiday week they were on strike.
The union also said it secured "firm contract language effectively stopping sub-contracting of normal maintenance work in house," according to a UAW settlement highlight sheet distributed to workers.

The job additions roughly match what union officials had demanded to ease overtime burdens when the strike began. GM has said it cannot add workers because the next-generation full-size pickup truck will require about 30 percent fewer workers.

However, analysts have said the strike cost the Pontiac East plant its position as the lead facility in producing the next-generation pickup truck. Mike Robinet, managing director of CSM Forecasting Inc., a Farmington Hills, Michigan, consultant, said GM's Oshawa, Ontario, plant may take over that position.

Officials from two other UAW locals said talks would continue through the weekend at key parts plants in Michigan and Indiana to hammer out new contracts before strike deadlines at 11:59 p.m. July 22.
A recording at Local 663 in Anderson, Indiana, said talks remained slow Friday with little progress on issues such as outsourcing and health and safety issues.

"Management continues to show no flexibility to resolve the critical issues," the recording said. "The shop committee will do whatever it takes to get a fair and equitable agreement that will ensure the membership's future at this plant."
About 2,500 workers from Local 663 work at a Delphi Interior and Lighting plant. They produce tail lamps and brake lights for nearly all GM vehicles.

Al Benchich, president of Local 909 in Warren, Michigan, said the union still hopes to reach an agreement before the Tuesday strike deadline. Benchich said he is encouraged by the terms of the Pontiac settlement.
"I think that lets our management know if they got certain things, we should expect to get some of the same things," he said.

Local 909 has about 2,800 members who work at the company's critical Warren, Michigan, transmission plant. The facility produces four-speed automatic transmissions for cars and light trucks, including GM's minivans.
